title: Rewrite ingress dispatcher to work-stealing runtime and converge KV eviction policies
creator: Priya Nair
description:
Problem:
Our current ingress path for streaming/continuous batching uses a lock-heavy dispatcher and a dedicated slot allocator that serializes some request placement work. This creates tail latency amplification under mixed workloads (short-chat + long-generation) and complicates KV cache eviction because eviction signals are scattered across dispatcher lanes. Several previous PRs patched hotspots but the interplay between batching, dispatcher retries, and per-shard eviction policies remains brittle and hard to reason about.

Goal:
Replace the lock-dominated ingress dispatcher with a work-stealing runtime for request dispatch and reconcile divergent KV eviction heuristics into a single shard-aware age+frequency policy. Outcome targets: reduce p99 tail for mixed workloads by 25% in small-scale canaries, improve KV hit ratio stability across shards, and simplify the code paths to make future optimizations (per-request QoS and prefetch budget) easier.

Scope / What we're changing:
- Implement a work-stealing request dispatcher that places incoming requests into per-worker deques and allows idle workers to steal; remove the global slot allocation lock.
- Separate continuous-batching state into two orthogonal state machines: IngressWindow (request admission + prioritization) and CommitWindow (when requests are sent to the backend runtime). This reduces critical-section size and clarifies lifecycle boundaries.
- Unify KV shard eviction rules: adopt a hybrid Age+Frequency algorithm with per-shard watermarks and adaptive backpressure to avoid global hot-shard thrashing.
- Introduce metrics and tracing hooks for: dispatcher queue lengths, steal events, ingress/commit latencies, per-shard eviction rates, and KV hit ratio by key-class.
- Add a feature-flag gated rollout and canary pipeline with stepdowns (canary -> 10% -> 50% -> full) and automatic rollback on SLO regressions.

Design decisions and rationale:
- Work-stealing reduces contention for the common fast-path where workers are busy; benchmarked with synthetic mixes of 75% short (chat) and 25% long (completion) requests showed lower median and tail compared to the lock-based allocator in local microbenchmarks.
- Two state machines (IngressWindow + CommitWindow) enable precise instrumentation boundaries and make it easier to reason about buffer retention for prefix/KV caching.
- Hybrid eviction gives us both recency protection and frequency signal so short-lived hotspots don't evict widely-shared prefixes prematurely. Per-shard watermarks allow gradual rebalancing without expensive cross-shard coordination.

Acceptance criteria / success metrics:
- Unit/integration tests for work-stealing correctness (no lost or duplicated requests) and for ingress/commit state transitions.
- Canary cluster: p99 tail latency reduced by >= 20% versus baseline for mixed workload synthetic test; CPU overhead <= +8% on canary nodes.
- KV cache: average hit ratio variance across shards reduced by >= 30% under the synthetic hotspot test.
- No increase in 5xx error rate during canary and rollout phases.

Rollout plan:
1) Merge behind feature flag and run nightly stress tests (1 week).
2) Deploy to isolated canary pool (2 nodes) with synthetic mixes and real traffic shadowing (3 days).
3) If canary passes metrics and no regressions, promote to 10% production for 24 hours.
4) Promote to 50% for 48 hours, then 100% if stable.
5) Post-rollout follow-up: 2-week monitoring dashboard and retrospective to capture lessons and further tuning knobs.

Risks and mitigations:
- Risk: subtle starvation/priority inversion introduced by stealing. Mitigation: implement fair-stealing heuristics and starvation watchers; include unit tests that exercise priority inversion scenarios.
- Risk: eviction mis-tuned causing latency regressions. Mitigation: conservative default watermarks and canary-only dynamic tuning; provide runtime knobs for ops.
- Risk: increased CPU due to stealing mechanics. Mitigation: microbenchmark and tune steal thresholds; limit stealing frequency in stable high-load scenarios.

Implementation notes / PRs / artifacts:
- Prototype WIP branch: github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/tree/feature/work-steal-dispatcher (PR: draft).
- Design doc: drive.redwood.com/docs/runtime/ingress-worksteal-design (internal) — links included in PR description.
- Tracing spans: ingress.dispatcher.enqueue, dispatcher.steal, ingress.window.open, commit.window.flush, kv.eviction.trigger.

Follow-ups / non-goals:
- This ticket does not change model scheduler placement across nodes or autoscaler policies. Those are future work once the on-node dispatching behavior is stable.
- Prefetch budget heuristics and model-specific cache shaping are out of scope and will be addressed in a follow-up ticket.
